clinicalPearls: A very rare, slowly progressive central nervous system disorder caused by persistent rubella virus infection of the brain
It arises years to a decade or more after congenital rubella syndrome, and less commonly after childhood-acquired rubella
Onset is usually in the second decade with insidious cognitive and behavioural decline, deteriorating school performance, and dementia
This is followed by progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, myoclonus, and seizures, culminating in severe neurological disability
Cerebrospinal fluid shows a raised protein and oligoclonal bands with markedly elevated rubella-specific antibody, reflecting intrathecal antibody production
Imaging typically shows diffuse white-matter change and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, with cerebellar involvement often prominent
There is no effective specific treatment, and its near-elimination follows widespread rubella vaccination and prevention of congenital rubella
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive rubella panencephalitis reflects long-term persistence of the rubella virus within the central nervous system after congenital or, rarely, postnatal infection. The virus is not fully cleared and continues a smouldering, low-grade infection of brain tissue over many years. A chronic immune-mediated process, with intrathecal synthesis of rubella-specific antibody, accompanies slowly progressive destruction of both grey and white matter, hence panencephalitis. There is widespread neuronal loss, gliosis, perivascular inflammation, and a characteristic prominent involvement of the cerebellum, producing the ataxia that is a notable feature. The mechanism resembles that of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis after measles, in that a common childhood virus persists in the brain and drives a delayed, progressive, and ultimately fatal encephalitis.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic viral encephalitides in the immunocompromised
Late complications of congenital infection from other agents
Inborn errors of metabolism presenting in adolescence
additionalInvestigations: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing raised protein, oligoclonal bands, and greatly elevated rubella-specific antibody
Paired serum and CSF rubella antibody indices to demonstrate intrathecal synthesis
MRI of the brain to show white-matter change and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy
Electroencephalography, which shows diffuse slowing without the periodic complexes of SSPE
Detailed history of congenital rubella syndrome or prior rubella infection
Exclusion of measles and other progressive encephalitides
redFlags: Relentless cognitive and motor decline in a young person with a history of congenital rubella
Loss of independent function and swallowing safety
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive and ultimately fatal, evolving over years to profound neurological disability and death, with no proven treatment able to halt its course.
pitfalls: Confusing it with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, as the two are clinically and mechanistically similar but follow different viruses
Overlooking a distant history of congenital rubella when assessing adolescent cognitive decline
Expecting the periodic EEG complexes of SSPE, which are absent in progressive rubella panencephalitis
Attributing the decline to a primary neurodegenerative disorder and missing the raised CSF rubella antibody
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
